lessons.title: Collection transformations
lessons.summary: If the predicate keeps odd values instead, what is the result?
explanation: filter on a List keeps elements satisfying its Boolean predicate. map creates the transformed result values. These collection operations evaluate eagerly and do not mutate the original list. Here n names each lambda argument explicitly.

Keeping even values from 1, 2, 3, 4 leaves 2 and 4. Mapping each to ten times itself produces 20 and 40. The returned List exposes a read-only interface; read-only is not a universal guarantee of deep immutability.

lessons.title: Lazy sequences and repeated work
lessons.summary: If the second toList call is removed, what is the final calls count?
explanation: asSequence creates a lazy processing view over the list. map runs as a terminal operation such as toList requests elements. It can avoid intermediate lists, but overhead means it is not automatically faster for small workloads.

This list-backed sequence can be traversed repeatedly; each traversal applies the mapping again. Not all sequences are reusable: some are constrained to one traversal. The counter below is a deliberate local illustration of repeated work, not a recommendation to depend on side effects in transformations.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin


fun main() {
    var calls = 0
    val values = listOf(1, 2).asSequence().map { n -> calls++; n * 2 }
    println(calls)
    println(values.toList())
    println(values.toList())
    println(calls)
}
```

Expected output or behavior: 0
[2, 4]
[2, 4]
4. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Destructuring and components
lessons.summary: If the destructured variables are renamed to duration and topic in that order, what prints using those names in the same order?
explanation: val (label, minutes) = session calls component1 and component2 in order. Data classes generate these functions according to constructor-property order. Variable names in the destructuring declaration do not select fields by matching their names.

An underscore skips a component you do not need. Destructuring is a concise way to bind values, not a deep copy of an object graph. Here String and Int values make the resulting bindings easy to trace.

}

lessons.title: Files and explicit encodings
lessons.summary: If appendText is replaced by writeText on the second operation, what remains?
explanation: java.io.File is a JVM API; the writeText/readText extensions belong to Kotlin’s JVM library. This is not a promise of identical APIs on Android, Native or JS. Run the example only in a disposable working directory: it creates or replaces notes.txt.

Charsets.UTF_8 maps the text to bytes explicitly. writeText overwrites the file by default; appendText adds text at the end. The extensions manage their streams, but I/O failures can still throw exceptions. Reading the whole file is suitable only when its size is bounded.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
import java.io.File

fun main() {
    val file = File("notes.txt")
    file.writeText("A", Charsets.UTF_8)
    file.appendText("é", Charsets.UTF_8)
    println(file.readText(Charsets.UTF_8))
}
```

lessons.title: Regular expressions and whole-input matching
lessons.summary: If both inputs change to "12", what prints?
explanation: Regex("[0-9]+") describes one or more ASCII digits. The bracket expression selects one digit; + requires at least one repetition. This deliberately excludes signs and whitespace, and does not prove that the numeric value fits Int.
matches requires the whole input to match. containsMatchIn asks whether any matching substring exists. For x12, the digit substring exists even though the complete input is not all digits.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin


fun main() {
    val digits = Regex("[0-9]+")
    println(digits.matches("x12"))
    println(digits.containsMatchIn("x12"))
}
```

true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: JVM dates and time zones
lessons.summary: If the instant becomes 12:30 UTC on the same day, what dates print?
explanation: The JVM java.time.Instant represents a point on the time line. ZoneId supplies rules for presenting that instant as local calendar time. Converting with atZone preserves the instant, not necessarily its displayed date.

At 00:30 UTC on January 1, New York is still on December 31. toLocalDate extracts the date from each zoned representation. This example uses JVM java.time rather than claiming a multiplatform date API or reading the current clock.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId

fun main() {
    val instant = Instant.parse("2025-01-01T00:30:00Z")
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("UTC")).toLocalDate())
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")).toLocalDate())
}
```

Expected output or behavior: 2025-01-01
2024-12-31. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Packages and visibility
lessons.summary: If label in Labels.kt becomes private, can Main.kt still call it?
explanation: The helper below belongs to package study, so import study.label makes its function available by its short name. A package declaration—not a folder name alone—determines the qualified name. Imports do not fetch code.

package study
fun label(): String = "review"

lessons.title: Suspend functions versus threads
lessons.summary: If answer() is called directly from this ordinary main without runBlocking, what happens?
explanation: suspend is a Kotlin language modifier allowing a function to call suspending operations. It does not automatically start a thread, choose a dispatcher or make a blocking call nonblocking. This answer function returns immediately but must still be called from a suspending context.

runBlocking from the separate kotlinx.coroutines 1.8.0 dependency creates a coroutine scope and blocks the calling thread until it finishes. Here it bridges a tiny command-line main; it is not a recommendation to block a UI or call runBlocking inside existing suspending code. Its braces supply a suspending lambda with a scope receiver. On this Unix-like JVM setup, set COROUTINES to the actual path of kotlinx-coroutines-core-jvm.jar version 1.8.0, then compile kotlinc Main.kt -jvm-target 21 -include-runtime -cp "$COROUTINES" -d app.jar and run java -cp "app.jar:$COROUTINES" MainKt. The classpath separator here is a colon; this command does not download anything.
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Structured coroutine scopes
lessons.summary: If the child assigns "finished", what does the print after coroutineScope report?
explanation: coroutineScope is a suspending function that does not finish until its child coroutines finish. launch starts a child and returns a Job rather than a value result. In these builders the implicit scope receiver lets you write launch without an explicit this.

The child writes result, and the print occurs after coroutineScope returns. With the inherited runBlocking context this child is not an uncoordinated worker thread. The example makes no claim about arbitrary launch order. A normal scope also propagates child failure; it is not an unmanaged global job.

lessons.title: Async results and awaiting
lessons.summary: If the right async result is 10, what is the total?
explanation: async starts a child coroutine and returns Deferred<T>. await suspends until that result is ready, then returns it or propagates its failure. async is a scope extension, not a keyword and not part of the Kotlin standard library.

lessons.title: Cooperative cancellation
lessons.summary: If the finally message changes to "released", which order is guaranteed?
explanation: A Job cancellation is a request, not a forced thread kill. Suspending library functions check cancellation; CPU loops must also cooperate, for example with ensureActive. Do not swallow CancellationException as an ordinary successful result.

CompletableDeferred<Unit> is a one-shot completion signal: complete(Unit) releases await without carrying useful data. The child then waits in awaitCancellation, which suspends until cancelled and never returns normally. cancelAndJoin requests cancellation and waits for cleanup. finally runs during this exit; it must not start suspending cleanup without an appropriate explicit policy.

Expected output or behavior: cleanup
done. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Mutexes and shared state
lessons.summary: If each worker repeats 25 increments, what prints?
explanation: count++ reads and writes a mutable Int; multiple workers need coordination. Mutex.withLock holds the same coroutine mutex around that entire update and releases it on exit. Waiting for this mutex suspends a coroutine rather than using a JVM monitor wait; a mutex is not reentrant.

Dispatchers.Default permits work on a shared pool of worker threads. coroutineScope waits for both launched children before the final print. repeat(2) runs its lambda twice, creating two workers; each performs 100 protected increments. No timing measurement or unprotected counter variant is used.
Expected output or behavior: 200. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Java platform types and null boundaries
lessons.summary: If the property is set to "read" before retrieval, what prints?
explanation: A Java method without sufficiently specific nullability information can appear as a platform type, often displayed as String! in tooling. The exclamation form is not Kotlin source syntax. Assigning such a result to a non-null Kotlin type can fail at runtime if Java returns null.

System.getProperty can return null when a property is absent. This isolated JVM fixture first clears its uniquely named property, then assigns the result to String?. The safe call plus Elvis operator handles absence without !!. These changes affect only this short-lived process, not an operating-system environment variable.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin


fun main() {
    val key = "codequest.lesson.optional.topic"
    System.clearProperty(key)
    val topic: String? = System.getProperty(key)
    println(topic?.length ?: -1)
}
```
Expected output or behavior: -1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: A resilient study-session pipeline
lessons.summary: If the first input changes from "15" to "70", what is collected and totaled?
explanation: flowOf emits its supplied values in order when collected; this fixed source contains four text inputs. mapNotNull applies toIntOrNull and drops null conversion results; filter retains only minutes in the inclusive range 1 through 60. This explicitly chooses to omit invalid items rather than pretending they were valid zero-minute sessions.

take(2) permits at most two accepted values to reach toList. toList is the suspending terminal collection; sum totals the resulting small list, safely bounded here by 120. This is an in-memory teaching pipeline, not persistent storage or a production error-reporting policy. In a real app, decide how rejected inputs should be reported to the user.

35. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
